title: US approves sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine
description: The US has approved the sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine, a critically-needed munition for defence against escalating Russian aerial attacks, a
body: The US has approved the sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine, a critically-needed munition for defence against escalating Russian aerial attacks, after Kyiv said deliveries had been delayed in recent months.The US State Department said the advanced PAC-3 interceptor missiles would cost $2.1bn (£1.6bn) and would be "funded entirely" by Kyiv's allies in Europe and Canada.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has repeatedly urged the US to speed up deliveries of its Patriots - the only effective weapon in downing Russia's deadly ballistic missiles.The latest move comes just days after a row between Zelensky and Donald Trump, with the US president saying it was time for Ukraine to get a new leader to try to end the war with Russia.In Friday's statement, the State Department said "this proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic stability in Europe".It said "Ukraine will pay for this purchase with donations from Canada, Germany, and Norway via the JUMPSTART program and national funds, financed by the European Union's Ukraine Support Loan". The statement said the "principal contractor" would be American company Lockheed Martin, adding that "no US funds are involved in this sale".Zelensky said earlier this week that his country had been waiting almost a month for the US to sign off on critical missile supplies.And in a Telegram post late on Friday, the Ukrainian president reported that earlier in the day Russian ballistic missiles had struck two of the country's regions."They continue to carry out terrorist strikes against our cities," he said. Zelensky has recently admitted that Ukraine was running critically low on Patriots, as Russia was intensifying its attacks on key energy infrastructure ahead of winter.Kyiv desperately needs the interceptors but there is a global shortage of the munitions due to their use by the US in its war against Iran.It is not clear what the production schedule will be for the Patriots - but it is  understood the order is for new builds rather than existing missiles, meaning there is unlikely to be any kind of rapid delivery to Ukraine.Patriots also have lengthy production times, with only 600 missiles produced per year according to the US Department of Defence.In July, Trump said Washington had "not agreed" to license Ukraine to produce Patriots - three weeks after offering the country such a right.

schema.headline: US approves sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine

title: Russell Brand accusers 'haunted' for years by alleged crimes, court hears
description: Some of the women in Russell Brand's rape and sexual assault case have been "haunted" for years by what they allege he did to them, jurors have been t
body: Some of the women in Russell Brand's rape and sexual assault case have been "haunted" for years by what they allege he did to them, jurors have been told.In her closing speech at London's Southwark Crown Court on Friday, prosecutor Reil Karmy-Jones KC said the women had "nothing to gain" from coming forward apart from "some closure".Speaking for the defence, Polly Dyer told jurors Brand had pleaded guilty and been fined over possession of cannabis in 1995, but had no other "convictions, cautions, reprimands or warnings". Brand, 51, is on trial facing seven charges; three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one allegation of attempted indecent assault. He denies the charges.Karmy-Jones KC told the court that this case brings together six different women, none of whom knows each other.She said that while all the alleged victims have since moved on with their lives, due to this trial they have been forced to "relive what has happened to them".None of the women involved has "sought the limelight" or "any kind of publicity", she said, adding there was "no benefit to them from perhaps some closure."Referring to Brand's accusers' evidence the prosecutor said "how many said he was nice and then there was a like a personality change…"His eyes changed, he snapped, from charming to frightening to nasty," Karmy-Jones KC said.She added that the complainant's evidence had been that "he didn't listen when I said no, he didn't stop, he didn't care, pulling pushing… thrusting"."In the rape cases, he kept on going until he achieved his ultimate aim."The prosecutor also dismissed the idea that a documentary had caused the women to "re-invent" what actually happened."There is no magic force in this documentary", she added."What in fact happened was these women have realised they are not alone and have bravely come before you to tell the truth."She added: "Truth they have lived with, which in some cases has haunted them for years."She told the jury: "The experience of people raped may be something that looms a little bit larger in your mind rather than the intricacies of the outfit."The defendant couldn't really remember anything when he was interviewed, in stark contrast to now when he suddenly seems to remember all sorts of details about the week."Addressing Brand's presented change in character, Karmy-Jones KC told the court "He may now be a completely different person to the man he was between 1999 and 2009."She added: "He may well look back and not find some of his jokes funny"."He may now treat women with kindness and consent".Brand's wife Laura gave evidence yesterday, when she told the court her husband was a "kind and a wonderful father".Karmy-Jones KC called her Russell Brand's "undoubtedly lovely wife", who "bravely" gave evidence.However, she also noted that she was not with him at the time many of the alleged acts are said to have taken place."The reality is she wasn't there then, for the first five counts, she wasn't with him, nor was she with him for the final two counts.""Any contact was, I believe, sparse."In the final set of agreed facts in his trial, the court heard from Dyer about Brand's fine after he "pleaded guilty to one charge of possessing cannabis on 20 April 1995"."He received a fine. He has no other convictions, cautions, reprimands or warnings", she said.The trial continues.

schema.headline: Russell Brand accusers 'haunted' for years by alleged crimes, court hears

title: Canada stops using 'avalanche dogs' for rescues in Rocky Mountains, stirring outrage
description: Scott Ward can still recall the relief he saw on parents' faces when a search and rescue dog he was working with found their children safe in Canada's
body: Scott Ward can still recall the relief he saw on parents' faces when a search and rescue dog he was working with found their children safe in Canada's vast and heavily wooded Banff National Park.Another time, his canine partner led him hiking up a steep mountainside for two hours until they reached a man with a broken leg who was close to dying from hypothermia.Now 73 and retired, Ward spent 17 years as a dog handler in the wilderness of the Canadian Rocky Mountains, work he described as gratifying.Over the years, the rescue programme was cut back to just one person in the role, and Ward was shocked when he heard recently that Parks Canada will end the programme entirely as of this month. Prime Minister Mark Carney's government is making broad funding cuts to Canada's public service, and Parks Canada announced last week that hundreds of their employees will soon be laid off. The agency confirmed the news to the BBC, calling it a "difficult decision" to axe its sole dog handler position out of Banff National Park, one of the most rugged parts of Canada that welcomes more than four million visitors each year from around the world. It added it is part of its efforts to modernise its law enforcement branch, and that "search and rescue operations will continue to be delivered" through other means.Cutting this one role has stirred public outrage, with more than 5,000 people signing a petition since Tuesday to restore it. William Stevenson, the Conservative Member of Parliament for the Banff area who started the petition, says he welcomes tighter government spending, but that this cut could harm public safety. "How could they possibly make such a bad choice in where to cut?" he told the BBC.The BBC has asked Parks Canada about how much the canine search and rescue programme cost to administer. For 55 years, the government used rescue dogs in the Canadian Rocky Mountains who were trained to trace "everything", Ward said, from a small paper clip to shell casings to a human body. After avalanches, a common winter hazard in the area, they were called upon to search for trapped hikers or skiers underneath heavy mounds of snow."It saves probers hours and hours of standing shoulder to shoulder and poking in the snow, and also exposing themselves to secondary avalanche hazards," Ward said.In the summer, they helped find children who got lost, often after wandering away from their parents' campsites. "We lost a huge public safety and staff safety resource," he said. Other countries still rely on canines, often called "avalanche dogs", for mountain search and rescue, including Italy, external. The last dog in Parks Canada's programme, a German Shephard named Leroy, was retired in August. For the seven years that he was on the job, Leroy helped track 156 people, find 57 who were lost in the wilderness, and solve two murders in Banff.A new canine was trained and ready for duty before Parks Canada gave notice last week that the programme would be eliminated as part of recent C$145m ($104m; £78m) budget cuts to Parks Canada, local newspaper Rocky Mountain Outlook reported.Along with his petition, Stevenson also raised the issue in Canada's parliament during a late sitting on Thursday. In response, Ryan Turnball, a Liberal MP and the parliamentary secretary for finance, said the government is focused on reducing Canada's deficit and "ensuring public funds support growth, resilience and the well-being of Canadians".Stevenson said he will continue to push on the issue, and has asked for a sit-down meeting with Parks Canada's CEO. As for Ward, he hopes that the programme will soon be restored. He recalled a quote that was often uttered by an old park warden who trained him: "You can make an armpit smell like a lilac bush and you can put a man on the moon, but nothing can replace the nose of the avalanche dog."

schema.headline: Canada stops using 'avalanche dogs' for rescues in Rocky Mountains, stirring outrage

title: Crypto giant Binance attempting to recover $6.3bn stolen in hack linked to North Korea
description: Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has frozen around half of the funds stolen in a "complex" hack, after $6.3bn (£4.7bn) wa
body: Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has frozen around half of the funds stolen in a "complex" hack, after $6.3bn (£4.7bn) was accessed in what is believed to be a record heist.The firm said $3bn of its stolen digital assets had been secured - but many were still in the hands of unidentified hackers. It initially thought an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing unauthorised withdrawals, but later said the attack was wider.Several analytics firms have linked the hack, which eclipses a $1.5bn (£1.12bn) heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025, to a North Korean hacking unit.The US Secret Service said it was "working around the clock" "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover" stolen funds.America's lead federal agency for investigating financial crimes added that it would "identify the cyber criminals responsible and bring them to justice", while Binance also said it was working with the FBI.While Binance said its US-facing exchange was unaffected, the US would still have jurisdiction to investigate the hack and help track down stolen funds - an effort which generally involves a global law enforcement effort.The hack also involved some US-linked assets, such as stablecoins Tether and Circle – cryptocurrencies pegged to the dollar.Binance told its users "your money is safe, and we're covering every loss".It had initially suspended all deposits and withdrawals - but then said in an update that "deposits remain unaffected".Binance's co-CEO Richard Teng said: "This was not carried out by one person. Our initial investigation suggested that the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop, however our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach."Teng also describes how the hackers used "a self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and traces as they went, making it more difficult for us to trace and investigate".Initially, the company had indicated the breach "may have started with a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop" but later statements have pointed to a broader breach.In a later update, the firm set it had "set aside" more than $6.34B in company funds to cover the stolen assets and was "actively buying" a range of crypto tokens.The Binance hack spooked cryptocurrency markets on Friday. The price of Bitcoin was down 5% to $76,800 in Friday afternoon trading in New York.Cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase was down 12% as investors also reacted to earnings results in which the firm reported revenue slightly below expectations. Robinhood, a financial services company that trades in cryptocurrency, was down 7.8%.Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide.The company said in 2024 that it had more than $160bn in assets under its custody.A lot of the fear right now from Binance users - and the crypto industry at large - is whether or not Binance will actually be capable of covering this enormous financial loss.The company has said repeatedly that customer funds will be covered and that the firm is strong enough to weather the storm.But crypto history watchers have been pointing out online that this is exactly the kind of message that FTX CEO Sam Bankman-Fried gave before his crypto exchange collapsed in 2022, leading to huge losses for customers and the industry.Several experts have warned customers not to regard Binance's promise to cover losses as legally binding and said they may need to pursue litigation to recover them.Daniel Tunkel, of the London-based Edwin Coe law firm, said that would "come down to what [customers] have been promised in their contracts", and "where Binance can be sued for non-performance, if it comes to it".Binance has been subject of regulatory scrutiny around the world.Meanwhile, AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said that several elements of the attack resembled earlier North Korean-linked incidents, including the Bybit hack.In the last five years the crypto industry has been beset by enormous losses from hackers.In nearly all cases investigators have blamed hackers from North Korea, pointing to the infamous Lazarus Group - also know as TraderTraitor. The names refer to clusters of cyber criminals accused of working directly for the regime.Chainalysis, a crypto analytics firm, said it had "high confidence" that a North Korean is linked to the hack.North Korea is an impoverished country with very little industry and heavy international sanctions and experts say the regime uses cyber crime as a way to bring money in.North Korea has always denied this, but the wealth of evidence from cryptocurrency flow analysis and insider interviews from defectors is compelling. It makes North Korea likely to be the only nation that uses hacking as a way to raise public funds.

schema.headline: Crypto giant Binance attempting to recover $6.3bn stolen in hack linked to North Korea

title: Police watchdog to investigate Met over letter about Meghan's father
description: The UK police watchdog is to investigate the Metropolitan Police's handling of a letter containing allegations against Thomas Markle that was handed t
body: The UK police watchdog is to investigate the Metropolitan Police's handling of a letter containing allegations against Thomas Markle that was handed to his daughter, the Duchess of Sussex, in 2019.The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said it had decided an investigation was required into the force's "failure to pass on allegations of serious offending... to relevant overseas authorities at the time".The letter, written by Markle's first wife Roslyn Loveless, is believed to have contained claims about Meghan's father. He has strongly denied recent allegations that he had possessed images of child abuse, describing them as "sick lies".On Thursday the Met said it had voluntarily referred itself to the IOPC.The letter at the heart of the IOPC investigation was sent to the Met's royal protection team by Loveless, who divorced Thomas Markle in 1975 and died in 2024.The handwritten letter was then passed to Meghan in January 2019, with the duchess saying last week that it had "made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father".Meghan did not provide any details but said it had given her sufficient reason to not visit Thomas Markle and not allow him to meet his grandchildren, Archie and Lilibet.Scotland Yard said the letter contained claims about offending outside the UK and that it had been forwarded to "the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness".The IOPC will consider why the Met did not share the contents of the letter with other law enforcement agencies, in the UK or overseas.The policing watchdog also said it had decided a further matter, relating to an alleged data breach in which information was passed on to a third party, "should be returned to the force to be appropriately dealt with". No details were provided about the circumstances of the alleged breach.The Met said on Thursday that it intended to make further referrals to "relevant overseas law enforcement agencies", a process which it expected to be completed "in the coming days".The letter was forwarded by officers to the Sussexes' royal office rather than to Meghan personally, while there have been reports that the Met did not keep a copy of the letter and had to ask for one from the Sussexes.The watchdog will have to consider how the contents of the letter were treated by the force at the time.Noel Rasmussen, Thomas Markle's granddaughter and niece of the Duchess of Sussex, previously told the BBC she was "deeply troubled by the questions surrounding the Metropolitan Police's handling of the information it received". "If allegations of this seriousness were brought to the attention of authorities, it is reasonable to ask what steps were taken [and] why the information was not shared with other law enforcement agencies."Reports of the Met's handling of the letter emerged as Thomas Markle's son had told the police in the Philippines about material which was alleged to contain sexual images of children, which he had claimed to have found in possessions belonging to Meghan's father.Thomas Markle had been in the Philippines in December 2025, undergoing hospital treatment, when Meghan wrote to him to end all contact.Authorities in the Philippines have begun investigating the claims. Police there have obtained a warrant to examine devices seized from Markle's former home.Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old videotapes were handed to police by Meghan's half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, last week. However, officers in Cebu needed a court warrant before they can examine the items.Thomas Markle Sr has strongly denied all the allegations against him. He has been backed by his daughter Samantha, who has dismissed the claims against her father as "fake".

schema.headline: Police watchdog to investigate Met over letter about Meghan's father

title: Police Scotland carrying out 'active inquiries' into  Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislane Maxwell Balmoral visits
description: Image source, Bav MediaImage caption, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has consistently denied any wrongdoingByMegan BonarBBC ScotlandUpdated 7 hours agoPol
body: Image source, Bav MediaImage caption, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has consistently denied any wrongdoingByMegan BonarBBC ScotlandUpdated 7 hours agoPolice Scotland is making inquiries into the activities of Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislane Maxwell during their time at Balmoral Castle. The Daily Express reported, external that the inquiry relates to allegations that women were trafficked to the royal residence in Aberdeenshire.Sex offender Epstein - who died in 2019 - and Maxwell, who was jailed in 2022 for sex trafficking, are understood to have visited the castle with Mountbatten-Windsor, who has previously denied any wrongdoing.Police Scotland said inquiries were at "a very early stage" and that it would be inappropriate to comment further.Representatives of Mountbatten-Windsor have been contacted for comment.Image source, US Department of JusticeImage caption, An image released by the US Department of Justice appears to show Epstein and Maxwell at BalmoralThe Royal family traditionally spend summer at Balmoral, where Queen Elizabeth II died in 2022.Asked about the Express report, a Police Scotland spokesperson said: "We have received information and active inquiries are ongoing but these are at a very early stage. "All inquiries are evidence led, with the needs of victim survivors at the heart of those inquiries. "We would never confirm details of ongoing inquiries and it would be inappropriate to comment further."In February, the force said it wanted to "speak to anyone with information" about Epstein's private jet using Edinburgh Airport.At the time officers said they had not received any reports or complaints in relating to the trip.Flight logs show Mountbatten-Windsor and Maxwell flew from Luton to Edinburgh on Epstein's private jet with two other passengers on 1 September 2006.An image believed to show disgraced financier Epstein and former socialite Maxwell at Balmoral was also released by US prosecutors during her sex trafficking trial.It is thought to have been taken in 1999, when Mountbatten-Windsor reportedly invited the couple to stay at the castle.Epstein and Maxwell were reportedly regular guests at royal residences in the late 1990s and early 2000s.Last year, the so-called Epstein Files were released by the US Department of Justice.Among them was an email from someone named 'A' to Maxwell which said they were at Balmoral and asked for "new inappropriate friends".The message, sent to Maxwell on 16 August 2001, begins: "I am up here at Balmoral Summer Camp for the Royal Family."Later in the email, the sender asks: "How's LA? Have you found me some new inappropriate friends?" before signing off "see ya A xxx".Image source, US Department of JusticeImage caption, A picture taken at Balmoral was released as part of the Epstein FilesJeffrey Epstein was 66 when he died by suicide in 2019 in a US prison while awaiting trial for sex trafficking charges. Maxwell, 60, was jailed for 20 years in 2022 for her role in procuring girls for Epstein.Last October it was confirmed Andrew had been stripped of his "prince" title and would be leaving his Windsor mansion, Royal Lodge.In February he was arrested on suspicion of misconduct in public office, in the wake of information that emerged from the Epstein files in the US, and later released.Earlier this month it emerged he was taking legal action against Thames Valley Police over search warrants issued before his arrest.Mountbatten-Windsor has consistently denied any wrongdoing linked to his association with Epstein.Asked about the latest reports, Scottish First Minister John Swinney said: "I understand the seriousness of the points that have been made and the concern that has been expressed."This is an operational matter for Police Scotland to fully and comprehensively investigate and I'm very confident that's exactly what Police Scotland will do."Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he did not want to comment on the police inquiries, which "should properly be independent".

schema.headline: Police Scotland carrying out 'active inquiries' into  Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislane Maxwell Balmoral visits

title: Mexico City Grand Prix practice result: Charles Leclerc fastest in Ferrari
description: Ferrari's Charles Leclerc headed McLaren's Lando Norris in Friday practice at the Mexico City Grand Prix.Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli, who is poised
body: Ferrari's Charles Leclerc headed McLaren's Lando Norris in Friday practice at the Mexico City Grand Prix.Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli, who is poised to clinch his first world title on Sunday, was fourth fastest behind team-mate George Russell.Only a victory by Russell or Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton can theoretically stop Antonelli becoming champion on Sunday. Even then, Antonelli only needs ninth place if Russell wins and 10th if Hamilton does.Leclerc, who topped both sessions on Friday, was 0.103 seconds quicker than Norris, with Russell just 0.003secs further adrift.Antonelli was 0.217secs off the pace, and ahead of the Red Bulls of Max Verstappen and Isack Hadjar.Leclerc's team-mate Lewis Hamilton was 11th overall after stopping on track with a technical problem before completing his qualifying simulation runs on the soft tyre.Behind Hadjar, Racing Bulls duo Arvid Lindblad and Liam Lawson sandwiched Pierre Gasly's Alpine, while McLaren's Oscar Piastri completed the top 10.Verstappen and Lawson face a trip to the stewards after a collision in the stadium early in the session.The first session was marked by 10 of the 11 teams running 'rookie' drivers in their cars.One of them was Cadillac's Colton Herta, who the team are considering promoting to a race seat in place of Valtteri Bottas next season.Initially, the team felt his running in Mexico had given him enough points under the F1 system to earn a 'superlicence', which is required to race in F1.But further investigation by governing body the FIA revealed the American nine-time Indycar race winner is still one point short and will have to complete one further practice session this year to secure his licence.The team plan to do that before the end of the season.

schema.headline: Mexico City Grand Prix practice result: Charles Leclerc fastest in Ferrari

title: Oleshky ceasefire: Hundreds evacuated from Russian-occupied town in Ukraine
description: Speaking to journalists on Friday evening, Lantratova put out a joint request with her Ukrainian counterpart "to the US First Lady... that humanitaria
body: Speaking to journalists on Friday evening, Lantratova put out a joint request with her Ukrainian counterpart "to the US First Lady... that humanitarian missions such as this one, delivering aid to residents in need, be conducted on a regular basis under the coordination of Mrs Melania Trump".A ceasefire - the longest and most widespread since the start of Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 - has been in force in the entire frontline region of Kherson since Tuesday, allowing for the road out of Oleshky to be demined.Residents who wished to leave had a four-hour window to do so on Friday. A convoy of 25 buses was brought in to allow up to 750 people to leave the town until 14:00 (12:00 GMT), along with ambulances for people with limited mobility.Several hundred people are understood to have decided to stay, despite the widespread devastation and the lack of gas, electricity and running water."Everyone who wishes to leave Oleshky will be given the opportunity to do so safely," Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said on Friday morning."At the same time, those who decide to remain will be able to stay and will receive all the necessary humanitarian assistance."Ukrainian military positions lie 5km (3.1miles) from Oleshky, but the evacuees will first have to travel into Russian-occupied territory and then to the southern Russian city of Anapa. They will board a Russian government plane to Gomel in Belarus, and then drive across the border into Ukraine's Chernihiv region.Others are expected to choose to stay in Russian-occupied territory.Both Lubinets and Lantratova posted videos from Oleshky on their social media channels, saying people were given the chance to form two groups depending on whether they wanted to be taken to Russian-controlled territory or to Ukraine.In one video, Lubinets can be seen meeting tearful locals. "The problem is that a lot of people are staying," he can be heard saying. "I was told that it was their own choice, we will do everything possible for the humanitarian aid to arrive."Russia said on Thursday that it had prepared "dozens of tonnes" of aid for the residents who do not wish to leave, including food, medicine, hygiene products and fuel for generators.An Oleshky resident told the BBC she had decided against leaving because "they wouldn't take my animals, so that's it."Olena, who now lives in Kyiv, said her grandmother and wider family in Oleshky were also staying behind."The older generation does not want to leave," she told the BBC. "I've barely managed to persuade my father - and only because I've just had a baby, who he would never see otherwise." Olena's grandmother's sister died in Oleshky last winter. "She lost her legs after stepping on a landmine, covered in snow... People took her to the hospital in a garden wheelbarrow," Olena said."That's how locals transport all wounded and dead people in Oleshky to the hospital and the hospital's morgue: in garden wheelbarrows."

schema.headline: Oleshky ceasefire: Hundreds evacuated from Russian-occupied town in Ukraine

title: Jamie Carragher sued: Aston Villa to take legal action against pundit over 'unacceptable insults'
description: Aston Villa say they will initiate legal action against Jamie Carragher over what the club branded as "unacceptable insults".Posting on their social m
body: Aston Villa say they will initiate legal action against Jamie Carragher over what the club branded as "unacceptable insults".Posting on their social media on Friday, Villa released a statement signed by their chairman Nassef Sawiris accusing Carragher of insulting the Premier League side and its fans.It added the club would "not allow anyone to stop our ascension in English and European football".Speaking on the Stick to Football podcast, Carragher attracted criticism from Villa fans by suggesting their manager Unai Emery would be interested in becoming Manchester United's head coach.Michael Carrick's position at United is hanging in the balance after a dismal start to the campaign and Carragher said "Aston Villa will never be Manchester United"."Surely he would want that opportunity to manage a giant again," Carragher said. "There is a chain in football, whether you like it or not."So Real Madrid will take Manchester United's best player, they did it with [Cristiano] Ronaldo. "And there will be teams below Aston Villa, and they'll take their players or manager, so shut the [expletive] up Aston Villa fans. Aston Villa will never be Manchester United."Carragher, a football pundit for works for Sky Sports and American broadcaster CBS, has already commented on the backlash he recieved after he told the fans to shut up."It was a joke after the stick Villa fans have given me over saying Emery may fancy joining Man Utd," Carragher said on social media."I hope these clown clips show me praising Emery/Villa like I have done for years & saying how pleased I was you won [the 2026 Europa League] in Istanbul."

schema.headline: Jamie Carragher sued: Aston Villa to take legal action against pundit over 'unacceptable insults'

title: King visits Guyanese slave rebellion site on Caribbean tour
description: Image source, PAImage caption, The King and Guyanan minister Steven Jacobs at Independence ParkByDaniela RelphRoyal correspondentReporting fromGuyanaU
body: Image source, PAImage caption, The King and Guyanan minister Steven Jacobs at Independence ParkByDaniela RelphRoyal correspondentReporting fromGuyanaUpdated 51 minutes agoThe King has made a poignant visit to the site where a Guyanese slave rebellion was violently resisted by British authorities, making the stop during his tour of the Caribbean.He visited Independence Park in Georgetown to remember the Demerera Slave Rebellion of 1823, which saw an uprising by thousands of enslaved people. Accompanied by Guyana's Culture Minister, Steven Jacobs, he was told how hundreds of slaves were killed by colonial leaders during the rebellion and many of those who survived were executed close to where the King stood.Above the King was a sign that he took time to read."This ground was used as a public execution site," it said, "where enslaved persons...were condemned to death and hung."The moment of reflection was what Buckingham Palace had described as the King "not shying away from the UK's colonial legacy" and described today as a chance for the King to reflect on Guyana's history of slavery and resistance.In 2022, Charles described how he was on a personal journey of discovery and was continuing to "deepen my own understanding of slavery's enduring impact", in a speech at the opening of a Commonwealth summit hosted by Rwanda.Independence Park, which is now a sports ground, drew a crowd of dozens of schoolchildren. The King stopped to talk to many of them asking them about their homework, their holidays and if they'd had a day off school.Image source, PAImage caption, The King greeted local young people in Independence ParkOutside one of the King's engagements later in the day, a small but noisy group of protesters gathered.Many held placards saying "no apology will return what was stolen, reparations now" and "justice must not depend on wealth status and connections"."This great wealth was built on the backs of slavery," said protester, Guyanese politician, Terrence Campbell. "I do not want the British public to think that by me saying reparations can take various forms, it means that they do not have responsibility for reparations. They do, because the United Kingdom benefited tremendously from slavery."The King will not be apologising for the UK involvement in the slave trade during the visit, nor will he offer reparations - compensation from those countries who benefited from the slave trade - in line with the position of the UK government.This tour has seen a number of demonstrations so far but none have seriously disrupted the King's programme.Image source, ReutersRoyal tours often include cultural exchanges and the King's trip to Guyana saw an unusual mix up of musical styles.On the bandstand of Promenade Gardens in Georgetown, the bagpipes of the National Piping Centre could be heard alongside traditional Guyanese drummers in a collaboration of musical styles. Seven pipers from the National Piping Centre have been touring Guyana over the past week to learn more about the Guyanese musical traditions.As part of his visit on Friday, the King also shared a moment with a veterans from Guyana who fought for Britain in the Second World War during an event at the Commonwealth War Graves in the capital Georgetown.King Charles met Donald Grant, 99, who will celebrate his 100th birthday next week on November 3.He also spoke to James Samuel, 100, who is in a wheelchair, with the the King hearing how aged 19 he enlisted in the British Guiana Volunteer Force in 1943."What a great pleasure it is to see you on this occasion," the King told him.Image source, PAImage caption, Britain's King Charles smells a water lily as he visits Promenade Gardens, one of Georgetown's oldest public spacesThe King was waved off at the end of his state visit by Britain's High Commissioner to Guyana, Joseph Fisher, Guyana's Prime Minister Mark Phillips and a number of other dignitaries.His departure had a small ceremonial element with the Guyana Defence Force providing a guard of honour at Cheddi Jagan International Airport.

schema.headline: King visits Guyanese slave rebellion site on Caribbean tour

title: Celebrity Traitors comes to a climax in nail-biting final
description: Image source, BBC/Studio Lambert/Euan CherryImage caption, Seven celebrities remained at the start of the final episodeByIan YoungsCulture reporterUpd
body: Image source, BBC/Studio Lambert/Euan CherryImage caption, Seven celebrities remained at the start of the final episodeByIan YoungsCulture reporterUpdated 15 minutes agoSpoiler warning: This story reveals details of The Celebrity Traitors finalWe've had four weeks of suspense, suspicion and very suspect tactics, as some of Britain's biggest stars engaged in a battle of wits to win the most popular show on TV.The second series of The Celebrity Traitors reached its climax on Friday, with the 21 original contestants having been reduced to seven before the final.They were then whittled down to two winners - with the faithful duo of comedian Romesh Ranganathan and Heartstopper actor Sebastian "Bash" Croft emerging victorious.The players successfully banished the remaining traitors - Love Island host Maya Jama and YouTuber King Kenny - in dramatic fashion, and the winning pair shared the £83,000 prize for their charities.Image source, Paul Chappells/ Studio Lambert/BBCImage caption, Romesh Ranganathan and Sebastian "Bash" Croft celebrated with host Claudia WinklemanAs it happened: Relive the Celebrity Traitors finalWatch The Celebrity Traitors on BBC iPlayerGet all the reaction on Uncloaked on BBC iPlayerMore than 15 million people have been tuning in to this series.Kenny reached the final stage, the endgame, after turning on his fellow traitor Maya at the last round table.Kenny, Romesh and Bash were joined by singer James Blunt in the endgame, where the remaining contestants gather around a fire pit to decide whether they think there are any traitors left.When James and Kenny were tied in a vote for who was a traitor, Bash persuaded Romesh to banish Kenny instead of James - thereby securing victory for team faithful."Absolutely devastated. I was so close. I smelled the victory," Kenny seethed.However, he can take consolation from the fact his performance on the show has established him as a mainstream star.Image source, Euan Cherry/Studio Lambert/BBCImage caption, Traitors Kenny and Maya fell at the final hurdleIn a further twist, James chose another round of voting and was subsequently evicted himself, leaving Romesh and Bash as the last men standing."This might actually be the best day of my life," 24-year-old Bash said through tears of joy.Romesh reflected: "I just really hope my mum's proud. And also my youngest son Charlie, who wanted me to come on the show - dad won. Please show me some respect."The pair will split their winnings between two refugee charities, the Refugee Council and Choose Love.Image source, BBC/Studio Lambert/Paul ChappellsImage caption, The final six: Maya, James, Kenny, Romesh, Leigh-Anne and BashEarlier, actor Michael Sheen was murdered in the first action of Friday's episode. "I am incredibly disappointed," he said. "Gutted that I got so close to the end. It's been absolutely unforgettable."When the action reached the endgame, Little Mix singer Leigh-Anne Pinnock was swiftly banished after Kenny voted to remove her."I was thinking me and him had a mutual understanding, and now I feel so stupid," she raged.Meanwhile, James B was left rueing one final mistake in a long but noble catalogue of misjudgements throughout the series.The singer, who looked aghast when he was attacked by Romesh during the endgame, was then the only one to choose to banish again when it came to the final three.James was unaware that Romesh and Bash had both chosen to end the game - meaning he could have been a winner if he had done the same - but became the victim of his own choice to banish."I've loved trying to work it out, I've loved getting it wrong so often, I've loved the tiny moments when I've got it right," he said wistfully. "I've loved the game."Image source, BBC/Studio Lambert/Euan CherryImage caption, James Blunt helped retrieve the final prize money in a mission involving dynamite and helicoptersCelebrities who departed earlier in the series included ex-EastEnders actor Ross Kemp, model Jerry Hall, sitcom star Miranda Hart, comedian Joe Lycett, presenter Hannah Fry and former BBC journalist Amol Rajan.This series is also likely to be remembered for the two contestants who made the unorthodox decision to reveal themselves as traitors, before being summarily dispatched by their fellow players.First, actor Richard E Grant was so giddy to have received the tap on the shoulder that he blurted out his supposedly secret status in episode two.Comedian James Acaster, meanwhile, was the most reluctant traitor in the history of The Traitors, and unexpectedly gave himself up when he came under pressure at the round table in Thursday's penultimate episode.Aftermath of Acaster's admission Image source, Euan Cherry/Studio Lambert/BBCImage caption, James Acaster effectively banished himself in a novel twist in the showThere have been reports, external that filming of the scene was paused and he was checked by welfare staff after he became anxious.Asked about the reports, a BBC spokesperson said on Friday that the safety and welfare of those taking part was the "highest priority", and "players are closely monitored and supported throughout by production which includes a dedicated and experienced welfare team".Speculation about the round table being heavily edited was fuelled when eagle-eyed viewers noticed, external a shot of Romesh reacting in shock - apparently to James A's initial confession - which in fact seemed to have come from a later moment, after Romesh had voted for James by writing his name on the blackboard.In the episode, the sequence where the celebrities all voted for James in light of his admission was shown as a relatively quick and straightforward process, raising a question about what prompted Romesh's shocked look.TV critic Ian Hyland wrote, external: "The most damaging thing about the James Acaster incident could be that it revealed just how much the production team and editors get involved in #CelebrityTraitors."'A bit dull?'However, James A's bombshell did provide the programme with a twist to spark it to life after what some viewers saw as a mid-series lull.On Thursday, the Hollywood Reporter noted, external that the show had achieved record-breaking ratings - before asking: "Why, then, has much of the consensus on social media been that it's all felt a bit dull?"Some noted a shortage of true back-stabbing, double-crossing and explosive rows - the things, in other words, that viewers love the most - while the celebrities were more chummy and savvy than previous groups of castle dwellers.And while there was no shortage of big characters, this season lacked an equivalent to Alan Carr, the hugely popular and apparently hapless comedian who lied and murdered his way to an unlikely victory as a traitor last year.The drama ramped up in the final, though, and Friday's episode is likely to have been the most watched TV programme of the year.

schema.headline: Celebrity Traitors comes to a climax in nail-biting final

title: Ellie Kildunne: how Red Roses star ended up benched by England
description: She's the poster girl. She's the former World Player of the Year. She came second at BBC Sports Personality of the Year. She lit up the 2025 Rugby Wor
body: She's the poster girl. She's the former World Player of the Year. She came second at BBC Sports Personality of the Year. She lit up the 2025 Rugby World Cup. She's even got her own Barbie doll. So why didn't Ellie Kildunne start for England against the USA on Friday night?First of all she is human, let's not forget that. We're all allowed ups and downs. It's just that Kildunne's dip comes with the large spotlight of her being the Red Roses' household name.None of her team-mates come close to her popularity with fans both in and outside rugby union with her 239,000 Instagram followers. Her face and name are used for clicks by all the media, present company included.However, if you follow the sport and watch her play, no-one is undroppable.England suffered their first loss in four years to end their 41-Test unbeaten streak in Toronto against Canada. In that fixture and their previous match with the same opposition in Exeter, Kildunne, 27, was a target for the opposition. She was never given space, defenders stepped up, her arms were pulled and balls were spilt.When England head coach John Mitchell benched her after England's loss in Toronto he was clear that "it isn't disputed that she adds huge value".However, he went on to add: "She's just going through a difficult period at the moment, and it's important for us to help her through that."She wants to become consistent as well, and she'll get back. It's also important to create competition and to recognise that you have to become more consistent, especially when you're competing in the Red Roses."So it's really important to reinforce the behaviours that we think are necessary to our game, and that goes for everyone."The key word we can take from that is "consistent" - mainly because Mitchell said it twice.Kildunne remains one of the world's most phenomenal players when it comes to gainline success and metres gained. Much of this is due to poor opposition defence, but her statistics show a decline over the past three seasons at international level. It seems almost harsh to highlight as these are numbers other players could only dream of but she's also gone from beating an average of six defenders a game in 2024, to 4.2 in 2026.Kildunne has also conceded more penalties in 2026 than either of the previous two years. Some of these statistics, althought not all, are mirrored in her PWR performances last season.While Canada are not alone, it does appear they are one of the best teams at dealing with Kildunne's threats.In their drawn match in Exeter, Kildunne made 17 carries for 47 metres, an average of 2.8m, which is well below her usual standards. In Toronto she had the ball turned over twice - that was her joint-most in any England game.Emma Sing now appears to have some purchase on the England 15 shirt and it is well deserved. She is a different full-back to Kildunne, which is a bonus for the Red Roses.Sing has three PWR titles with her club side Gloucester-Hartpury and has been one of their most reliable players throughout that period. She has got a monster boot round the park and off the tee and, while Sing might not score the same worldies we have seen from Kildunne, her highlights reel is none too shabby.On Sing's starting selection in Ottawa, Mitchell was happy to explain the players' differences: "They play quite differently. So we're very fortunate to have two very good full-backs. But you know, Emma's been sitting in the in the wings in this particular phase of our campaign."She was intermittent through injury for a long period of time. So she's in a really good physical place, and she's worked really, really hard. So I think it's time to give her an opportunity."It is a bit crass, but if you only follow men's rugby, Kildunne is a bit more Marcus Smith, while Sing is a bit more Freddie Steward - they are just different players.Add to that, Sing was brought up on a Devon sheep farm and is not a huge fan of the media spotlight. That is not to say that Kildunne has coveted it, but she is far more comfortable in the media space.You also must tip your hat to Kildunne and how she has managed herself with her new-found fame. After England beat New Zealand at Allianz Stadium in September, she spent an hour signing autographs and doing selfies to an unrelenting, screaming chorus of "Ellie, Ellie, Ellie".Managing your own needs as an athlete and the increasing demands of fans is not an easy circle to square.So where does Kildunne go from here? That is actually the most exciting bit.No-one with a spiral bomb like she produced in the 2025 Rugby World Cup final is going to fade into the shadows. She is an incredible athlete and rugby player, so the expectation is that, much like Doctor Who, she will just regenerate.Kildunne 2.0 could end up spending more time on the wing for England initially, but you can only see her fighting for a shirt and getting better.

schema.headline: Ellie Kildunne: how Red Roses star ended up benched by England

title: 'Respected and beloved': Tributes pour in for Sir Patrick Stewart
description: Dame Judi Dench said she was "shocked" and "very sad" to hear of Sir Patrick's death, adding: "He's never been one of those actors who never felt like
body: Dame Judi Dench said she was "shocked" and "very sad" to hear of Sir Patrick's death, adding: "He's never been one of those actors who never felt like it that night, he was always very, very committed... He'll be much missed and he was much admired."George Takei, who played Hikaru Sulu in Star Trek, said the actor "inspired a whole next generation of star-gazers who looked longingly ahead to a brighter future for all humanity".Sir Patrick would later be celebrated for his portrayal of Professor Charles Xavier - most commonly known as Professor X - in the X-Men film franchise.Hugh Jackman, who starred alongside him in the franchise, called him a "tremendous friend and man", saying: "We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today."Sir Ian, a longtime friend of his X-Men co-star, who officiated his wedding in 2013, said Sir Patrick was "defined by being born and bred in Yorkshire"."You could hear it in his accented voice and in the stern honesty with which he told you what he thought and felt. Yorkshiremen have no truck with half-truths or avoidance of big issues."Sir Ian recalled first meeting Sir Patrick as young actors in the Royal Shakespeare Company (RSC) and how he had expressed caution over him taking on the Star Trek role."He took the risk and thank goodness for us all that he did," said Sir Ian, who appeared with Sir Patrick in a 2009 theatre production of Waiting for Godot.He added that while the US had become Sir Patrick's "adopted home", he "never forsook his origins" growing up in Yorkshire, and said "the proudest achievement of the most respected and beloved actor of his generation on either side of the Atlantic, was his appointment as chancellor of Huddersfield University".Sir Ian noted that Sir Patrick's final film appearance will be as Professor X in the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday film. Marvel Studios described him as "a singular talent, a generous collaborator and a true gentleman".The Academy dubbed his voice "unmistakable", adding: "Whether commanding the bridge of the Enterprise or guiding a generation of young mutants, Sir Patrick Stewart brought a tenderness to his characters that made us feel we knew them."Sir Patrick died on Wednesday "in the loving care of his wife", a statement from his family said. "We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace," it added.The veteran actor is survived by his wife, Sunny Ozell, as well as by his two adult children from his first marriage, Daniel and Sophie Stewart.Dame Harriet Walter, who first met Sir Patrick in his theatre days more than 40 years ago, said his passing was like a "huge giant tree has fallen in the forest"."He had fire in his eyes and you were absolutely in the room with him," the Succession actress told BBC Newsnight. "I've never heard a bad word against him. And I think the world's going to be very poor without him."Theatres in London's West End will dim their lights for two minutes on 3 November in his honour.  Hannah Essex, co-chief of the Society of London Theatre and UK Theatre, called him "one of the greatest stage actors this country has ever seen".As well as having roles in films such as Safe House, Robin Hood: Men in Tights and the original Dune, Sir Patrick continued to appear on TV throughout his career, making guest appearances on Frasier, Futurama and the Simpsons.US actor and animator Seth MacFarlane, who grew up as a fan of Sir Patrick, said he was "gifted the privilege of becoming a colleague and friend" as they worked together on Family Guy, American Dad! and Ted. MacFarlane described him as a "rare actor who could take any bit of dialogue and elevate it, making a good writer sound great and a great writer sound masterful".Comedian Ricky Gervais, whose BBC programme Extras Sir Patrick guest starred in, described him as a "legend".Sharing a video of the pair giggling in a set of bloopers for the series, Gervais said: "I still can't believe he agreed to do this scene. And he didn't even mind when I ruined every take."Sir Patrick was a lifelong supporter of English Football League club Huddersfield Town, which called him a "titan of his craft"."Fiercely proud of his Yorkshire roots, Sir Patrick was a Terrier in every sense, and we're proud to have counted him as one of our own," the club added.Alzheimer's is the most common type of dementia, while Lewy Body Dementia is another common form caused by abnormal protein deposits, which cause a loss of cognitive function.The Alzheimer's Society CEO Michelle Dyson said Sir Patrick was an "extraordinarily talented and much-loved actor, admired by millions around the world", adding: "His death is a heartbreaking reminder of the devastating impact dementia has on people and families across the globe."The actor became a campaigner on domestic violence in later life, including becoming an ambassador for domestic abuse charity Refuge in 2007, after witnessing his mother suffer violence at the hands of his father.Hetti Barkworth-Nanton, Refuge's board chair, said it had been a privilege to "watch his endless devotion" to the cause, adding that he "broke down barriers and taboos on the subject".Andy Burnham considered Sir Patrick to be "one of the very best" who "never forgot his working-class Yorkshire roots"."He brought joy to millions," the prime minister's spokesman said on his behalf. "He always stood up for what he believed in, including through his campaigning to help those affected by domestic violence.

schema.headline: 'Respected and beloved': Tributes pour in for Sir Patrick Stewart

title: We went on holiday with our neighbours and swapped families - it tore us apart
description: Image source, Rachel StoneImage caption, Rachel as a baby with her father Rex and brother Ian - and Rachel todayByEmily DoughtyUpdated 06:21 GMTRachel
body: Image source, Rachel StoneImage caption, Rachel as a baby with her father Rex and brother Ian - and Rachel todayByEmily DoughtyUpdated 06:21 GMTRachel Stone was five and her brother Ian was 10 when their mum and dad took them on a caravan holiday to Wales with the family next door.They spent two fun-filled weeks together - but when they got home, each family split in half and swapped houses.Rachel and her mother Kay moved in with the neighbour Eddie and his daughter Alison. Eddie's wife Irene and their daughter Dawn moved in with Rachel's dad Rex and her brother Ian.Rachel tells Dr Sian Williams, host of Radio 4's Life Changing podcast, of the trauma of her family being torn apart, the chaos that unfolded and how she has come to forgive her parents.Image source, Rachel StoneImage caption, Rachel's dad Rex and brother Ian remained in their old home, while she moved in next door with her motherRachel and Ian had initially been delighted when a new family moved in next door. "We instantly hit it off, all four of us." They were thrilled to be going on holiday together. Rachel remembers two caravans parked side-by-side and a trip up Snowdon (officially known as Yr Wyddfa). But when it was time to go home, everything was mixed up - people were getting in the wrong cars.Rachel remembers her mum leaning back from the passenger seat, saying: "'We're going to have a new family. We're going to be living in number eight with Eddie and Alison. Alison's going to be your new sister."And your dad and brother are still going to live in number 10. And Auntie Irene and Dawn are going to live there. And Dawn's going to be your brother's new sister."Rachel immediately felt "very panicked and afraid and upset" and says she started to cry.As the car rumbled along, she felt "bewildered, but also a little bit excited". She liked Alison and had always wanted a sister.That night, Alison let her sleep on her top bunk and the next morning the adults switched belongings between the houses in the Isle of Sheppey where they lived.Rachel says she felt very confused. "You can't help but think that it's your fault."Life ChangingMy family was 'jumbled up'28 October 2026Life at number 8, where Rachel now lived, was very different to number 10. Her old house had been clean, whereas this house had "dog hair, greasy things, car things".She describes her mum as "firm but fair" and very practical.Her stepdad Eddie "was never horrible to me, but I never called him dad. I wasn't his girl."She also missed Ian desperately. "I was very proud of him. He was my big brother."I used to wait in the front garden for him to come home from school when I was a toddler." Image source, Rachel StoneImage caption, Rachel, pictured here at nine years old, says life with her new family at number 8 was very different to her old life Rachel was seven when the two couples went to court together and got divorced. They later married their new partners in separate low-key registry office ceremonies. Rachel did not even know her dad had married Irene until she saw the wedding photo. Her visits to her old home tailed off when she was about 11 or 12. She says she found it difficult to go and visit her dad and did not get along with Irene. Meanwhile, life with her mum Kay and Eddie was chaotic."[He] was quite possessive and controlling. By the time we got to 13, she [Mum] said, 'it's not sustainable, [we] can't live like this".Image source, Rachel StoneImage caption, Rex and Kay on their wedding day. They went on to divorce and marry their neighbours Rachel said school was her "escape". She got good grades and became a teacher. She got married and had two sons but is now separated and works as a business coach.Throughout her life, Rachel's mother would never talk about the swap. "I asked a lot of questions. She told me it was complicated."Decades later, on a family holiday with her own sons, Rachel asked again."I said to my mum, 'Oh, Joseph's 10 now... Ian was 10 when you let him go with Dad and Irene.'"She says her mum was "beside herself with guilt and the shame... for her selfish decisions.""Years later she actually said to me - the words I almost wanted to hear all my life  - 'I'm so sorry I let you down and I want to try and make it up to you.'" Rachel says it was the start of her rebuilding a "wonderful" relationship with her mum. Image source, Rachel StoneImage caption, Despite being separated as children, siblings Rachel and Ian remain close Rachel never had a close relationship with her dad. "He told me he had a choice between his wife and his children. Unfortunately for me, he chose his wife."He and Irene stayed together until his death aged 81. But when she spoke at her dad's funeral, Rachel said she felt she owed him an apology."I imagined a character of a perfect dad that had been taken away from me... I created this superhuman being that could be everything."And I wanted him to be like that. But I also think you have to accept people for who they are."I think that parents do the best they can... You can't hope for your parents to be something they're not."Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.

schema.headline: We went on holiday with our neighbours and swapped families - it tore us apart

title: Eddie Howe to Man Utd? The fans, the finances, the football structure
description: What Howe could bring to Man Utd - and what are the challenges?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Eddie Howe has been out of work since leaving
body: What Howe could bring to Man Utd - and what are the challenges?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Eddie Howe has been out of work since leaving Newcastle United in the summerBySenior football correspondentUpdated 6 hours agoWhen Sir Jim Ratcliffe became a co-owner of Manchester United in 2024, much of the narrative centred on his desire to rebuild the club around a British core.Given the expense of buying homegrown players, and the difficulties Michael Carrick -  the first permanent British managerial appointment of the Ineos era - has faced this season, perhaps Ratcliffe is rethinking.But if Carrick fails to stop the rot and loses his job, United are already considering the merits of appointing another British coach - albeit one who is more experienced.That Eddie Howe is a contender for a job that remains one of the most high-profile in world football isn't hard to fathom.Speak to those who have worked alongside Howe and they describe a man whose track record of improving players is a direct result of his relentless approach on the training field.They will also tell you Howe is someone who places an unwavering importance on the methodology of setting a winning culture.Howe may lack experience at one of the traditional top-six clubs, but his body of work at Bournemouth and Newcastle is impressive.Having been appointed Bournemouth boss with the club facing relegation from League Two in January 2009, Howe led them to the Premier League in 2015. He went on to establish the Cherries as a top-flight club before leaving - for a second time - in 2020.In 2021, Howe was appointed Newcastle manager. He led them from relegation trouble to qualification for the Champions League on two occasions and won the EFL Cup - the club's first trophy in 56 years - in 2025.Mixed reception to Howe linksOf course, managing Manchester United is an altogether different proposition.Indeed, Howe's emergence as a potential successor to Carrick has been greeted with negativity in some circles.Sections of the fanbase have been vocal on social media with their opinion that Howe isn't a big enough name to replace Carrick.Former United players Paul Scholes and Nicky Butt also fell short of providing their backing to Howe on their podcast, though it is worth pointing out they spoke in favour of the 48-year-old's potential appointment when Ruben Amorim was sacked in January.Ex-captain Roy Keane is among those to have backed Howe as a possible successor to Carrick, and other former top-flight players - including Darren Bent, Gareth Barry and Jack Wilshere - have also touted him as the man for the job.Of course, if you look hard enough you'll find voices for and against every potential manager, and it will be up to United chief executive Omar Berrada, sporting director Jason Wilcox and director of recruitment Christopher Vivell to weigh up how they proceed.Their first decision will be what happens with Carrick, and Saturday's match against Chelsea is likely to have a bearing on how United move forward.Figure caption, 'I don't need any assurances'Finances a factor in Carrick's futureIf Carrick does depart, finances will inevitably be a factor.The former Middlesbrough boss and his staff will need to be paid up before United even get to factoring in the monetary commitment towards their next head coach.While the details of Howe's agreement with Newcastle when he left in the summer remain confidential, it is understood that as things stand any club or national team would be required to pay a seven-figure compensation fee to the Magpies. Multiple sources have told BBC Sport that Newcastle - with a view to protecting themselves against Howe walking straight into another club - reached an agreement over a compensation structure that decreases over time.It is understood that figure started at £6m but has already reduced by half.The compensation payments have an expiry date - understood to be before the end of the season - at which point he can be appointed for nothing.Of course, in an industry in which astronomical figures are the norm, the prospect of paying a maximum of £3m for Howe may not be too problematic.That said, given the amount Manchester United have spent on hiring and firing managers in recent years, it is understandable if Berrada and Wilcox want to keep costs down.Would Howe fit Man Utd's footballing structure? As well as the doubts from some supporters about Howe's potential appointment, there has also been conjecture over how he would fit in United's footballing structure.At both Bournemouth and Newcastle, Howe developed a strong powerbase in all aspects of the footballing department - including recruitment.That dynamic wasn't without financial benefit to Howe's employers.The likes of Nathan Ake, Callum Wilson and Tyrone Mings were all signed by Howe at Bournemouth - and sold for a big profit by the Cherries.At Newcastle, meanwhile, Howe was instrumental in the signings of Bruno Guimarares, Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and Alexander Isak - all of whom were sold for more than they joined for. Dan Burn, Lewis Hall and Tino Livramento are among those to have developed into full England internationals under his coaching.But with a football management structure at Old Trafford that includes Berrada, Wilcox and Vivell, it is likely that Howe - at least not immediately - would not be afforded the same level of autonomy.Howe, though, is on record saying he is happy to work alongside sporting directors, and has a track record of doing so - firstly at Bournemouth under Richard Hughes, then chief executive Neill Blake.At Newcastle, he worked closely with senior management figures Dan Ashworth, Amanda Staveley and Mehrdad Ghodoussi - so fitting into Manchester United's structure wouldn't be drastically different.Whether he would want the job given the challenges, we may never know. And ultimately it is the opinion of Manchester United's decision-makers that will truly matter.'An obvious contender to replace Carrick' - analysisByChief football news reporterHowe is an obvious contender for the Manchester United job, just as he would be if the England head coach's position became available.Whether he is offered it or not will give a clear indication about the path United are going down.Director of football Jason Wilcox is thought to favour the 48-year-old, with director of recruitment Christopher Vivell preferring former Bayern Munich and Germany coach Julian Nagelsmann.Ultimately, their recommendations will be assessed by chief executive Omar Berrada, with minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe and co-chairs Joel and Avram Glazer having the final say.It is not completely clear where the negativity about Howe moving to Old Trafford comes from, other than Wilcox being targeted by Manchester United fans during the 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth. In the current managerial climate, few managers get the chance to build a body of work at one club over a number of years as, for instance, Sir Alex Ferguson did at Aberdeen before he moved south in November 1986.There is clearly a general disillusionment among the club's matchgoing fans around the football decisions taken since Ratcliffe bought his minority stake in early 2024, but Erik ten Hag, Ruben Amorim and Michael Carrick have all been backed.Some say no manager can succeed at United with the structure as it is, and it is clear whoever is in charge needs to mould together a squad bought by six permanent managers, most of whom have differing playing styles.

schema.headline: Eddie Howe to Man Utd? The fans, the finances, the football structure
